passages.original: Is ergo primo mercaturam exercens, ad Indos profectus est, et brevi tantam divitiarum copiam sibi comparavit, ut deinde Alexandriam adveniens, se totum philosophiæ studio et Ægyptiorum disci- plinis tradiderit, atque mercatura relicta, Aristote- licam vitam imitari voluerit. Abundans itaque otio atque divitiis, acri simul pollens ingenio, nova, sed paradoxa dogmata in orbem inducere secum reputa- vit, Cujus quippe desiderii causa, Empedoclis, aiunt, sententiam secutus, duo rerum principia coæterna commentus est : unum bonum, malum alterum; illud Deum ac lucem, hoc materiam et tenebras appellavit; qui error fuit unum ex palmaribus dogmatibus Va- lentinianorum et Marcionitarum, secundo Ecclesiæ sæculo catholicam Christi religionem vexantium.
passages.english: He, then, at first engaging in trade, set out for the Indians, and in a short time acquired for himself so great an abundance of riches that afterwards, arriving at Alexandria, he gave himself wholly to the study of philosophy and to the learning of the Egyptians, and, having abandoned trade, wished to imitate the Aristotelian life. Abounding therefore in leisure and riches, and at the same time endowed with a sharp intellect, he resolved within himself to introduce into the world new but paradoxical doctrines. Indeed, because of this desire, following, they say, the opinion of Empedocles, he devised two co-eternal principles of things: one good, the other evil; the former he called God and light, the latter matter and darkness. This error was one of the chief doctrines of the Valentinians and Marcionites, who harassed the catholic religion of Christ in the second century of the Church.
passages.notes: The subject is Scythianus, the reputed forerunner of Mani, as the context indicates.

passages.original: In tanto ergo, tamque sublimi prosperæ for- tunæ statu constitutus, præcedentem suæ servitutis conditionem exhorruit, ac subinde veritus ne sibi cederet in opprobrium, rejecto Cubrici nomine, illud aliud Manetis sibi assumpsit. Quid vero istud voca- bulum apud Græcos potissimum significet, paucis descripsit Eusebius Cæsariensis dicens (Lib. VII Hist. Eccl., c. 27) : Quo tempore Manes quidam, secundum nomen insaniens, et instinctu dæmonis agitatus, invi- sam, et exsecrabilem omnibus hæresim docet; Pro insa- nia itaque Græci, ut ex eo Manetis nomine irridendi occasionem arriperent, illud interpretati sunt, ut post Eusebium Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus etiam testatus est (Cateck.
passages.english: Placed, then, in so great and so lofty a state of prosperous fortune, he came to loathe the former condition of his servitude, and soon after, fearing that it might turn to his disgrace, he rejected the name Cubricus and took for himself that other name, Manes. What this word chiefly signifies among the Greeks Eusebius of Caesarea described in a few words, saying (Book VII of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 27): "At that time a certain Manes, raving according to his name, and driven by the prompting of a demon, teaches a heresy hateful and execrable to all." The Greeks, therefore, so that they might seize from it an occasion for mocking the name of Manes, interpreted it as "madness," as after Eusebius Cyril of Jerusalem also testified (Catechesis
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-citation; the reference continues in the following context ("6"). The pun is on Greek mania, "madness".

passages.original: Age vero isthæc missa faciamus, aliud com- mentum indicaturi, quod laudato Epiphanio, Beau- sobre affingere conatur, occasione maritalis conjugii, a Scythiano cum femina superioris Thebaidis initi. Hanc enim captivam fuisse narrat (a) Archelaus, cui Socrates suffragatus est. Orientales autem non ab- horrere a captivis uxoribus etiam ipse Beausobre, aliquorum testimonio suffultus, asseverat. Sed occa- sionem inde arripit ut stylum contra Epiphanium vertat, quod pulchram et juvenem captivam in per- ditam infamemque meretricem convertere voluerit;
passages.english: But come, let us set these things aside, as we are about to point out another fabrication which Beausobre tries to pin on the Epiphanius we have cited, on the occasion of the marriage contracted by Scythianus with a woman of Upper Thebaid. For Archelaus relates that she was a captive, and Socrates supports him. And Beausobre himself, backed by the testimony of some [writers], asserts that Orientals did not shrink from captive wives. But he seizes the occasion from this to turn his pen against Epiphanius, because [Epiphanius] wanted to turn a beautiful young captive into an abandoned and infamous harlot;

passages.original: Hisce ergo sacrilegis atque superstitiosis jactis fun- damentis,alia dogmata (ait Eusebius)stulta et impia a diversis hæreticis,qui jam prius exstincti fuerant mutuata disseminans,catholicam religionem persisis venenis labefactavit,et prorsus corrupit.inter cæ- tera autem figmenta,ex marcione,Valentino,Carpo- crate,aliisque Gnosticæ auctoribus,mutuata, sequentia numerari solent : duo videcicet rerum om- nium esse principia,deum nempe et diabolum ;
passages.english: Having laid, then, these sacrilegious and superstitious foundations, "disseminating other foolish and impious dogmas borrowed from various heretics who had already died out" (says Eusebius), he undermined the catholic religion with Persian poisons and utterly corrupted it. Among his other fabrications, borrowed from Marcion, Valentinus, Carpocrates, and other authors of Gnostic [doctrine], the following are usually counted: namely, that there are two principles of all things, that is, God and the devil;
passages.notes: "persisis" read as "Persicis" (Persian); "videcicet" as "videlicet".

passages.original: Manetis agenti rationeem, in suæ hæreseos errores evulgandos, paucis primo Eusebius Cæsariensis de- scriptis dicens (lib. vn hist. ecclesiast. c. 27) : Elatus in insania (ait) ad similitudinem christi duodecim di- scipulos eligens ad prædicandum mittebat. Eusebio con- cinent omnes veteres sciptores, si unum excipiamus.
passages.english: Eusebius of Caesarea first described in a few words Manes' way of proceeding in spreading the errors of his heresy, saying (Book VII of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 27): "Carried away in madness," he says, "choosing twelve disciples in the likeness of Christ, he sent them out to preach." All the ancient writers agree with Eusebius, if we except one.

passages.original: 40 Et quidem ad rem nostram claribeus et expres. sius non poterat Augustinus, ita scribens (lib. de Hæresibus cap. 46) : Unde ses in suis litteris, Jesu Christi apostotum dicit, eo quod Jesus Christus se mis- surum esse promiserat,atque in illo miserit Spiritum sanctum. Propter quod etiam ipse Manichæus duodecim discipulos habuit, ad instar apostolici, quem numerum Manichæi hodieque custodiunt. Non aliis quoque phrasibus usus est Theodoretus, de hæreti- corum disserens fabulis, cum paucis hisce verbis a Manete discipulorum factam electionem et illius pseudochristi imitationem descripsit (Lib.1 Hæret.
passages.english: And indeed Augustine could not have spoken more clearly and expressly to our point, writing thus (Book on Heresies, chapter 46): "Hence in his writings he calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ, because Jesus Christ had promised that he would send [the Paraclete], and sent the Holy Spirit in him. For this reason Manichaeus himself also had twelve disciples, after the pattern of the apostolic [number], a number which the Manichees keep even today." Theodoret too used no other phrases when, discussing the fables of the heretics, he described in these few words the election of disciples made by Manes and his imitation as a pseudo-Christ (Book I of the Heretical
passages.notes: Breaks off mid-reference (Haereticarum Fabularum). "ad instar apostolici" presumably for "apostolici numeri".

passages.original: Ephræm confirmari assiverat, qui antequam ex præsentis lu- cis usura migraret, cuidam Simeoni benedictionem dare cupiens, ita effatus est : Tamquam medicus in castris, ita nomen tuum pervadat orbem terrarum. Qui dicendi modus, apud Orientales in proverbium, seu commune venisse adagium Beausobre sibi blanditur. cum medicinæ facultas, auctore Strabone, ad hominis conservationem ordinata sit. His omnibus se adjicere posse affirmat Scythianum, quem fama Manetus ma- gistrum fuisse tradit , medicinæ institutionibus va- casse, et Hieracem, unem ex duodenis Manichaicis discipulis, huic disciplinæ studium applicuisse.
passages.english: [Beausobre] asserted that this is confirmed from Saint Ephrem, who, before departing from the enjoyment of this present light, wishing to give a blessing to a certain Simeon, spoke thus: "Like a physician in the camp, so may your name pervade the whole world." Beausobre flatters himself that this manner of speaking had passed among the Orientals into a proverb, or common adage, since the art of medicine, on the authority of Strabo, is ordered to the preservation of man. To all these [points] he affirms that he can add that Scythianus, who report says was the teacher of Manes, devoted himself to the teachings of medicine, and that Hierax, one of the twelve Manichaean disciples, applied his study to this discipline.
passages.notes: Subject supplied from context. "Manetus" read as "Manetis".

passages.original: Siquidem aliquot male partos novi Testamenti libros, et eos forte, quos Valentiniani aliique hæreticorum corruperant habere potuit, cum jam eruditis notum sit Christianos catho- licos ad integre servandos canonis libros multum operis adhibuisse ; ne videlicet ethnici illos igni tra- derent, ut narrat Eusebius ; et ne hæreticorum prin- cipes eos corrumperent et depravarent ; quemadmo- dum ex libro Constitutionum quæ apostolis tribun- tur jam factum fuisse colligimuq, de quibus ipsi opportunius sermonem habebimas.
passages.english: For he could have had some books of the New Testament wrongly acquired, and perhaps those which the Valentinians and other heretics had corrupted, since it is already known to the learned that catholic Christians took much trouble to preserve the books of the canon intact: namely, that the pagans should not consign them to the fire, as Eusebius relates; and that the leaders of the heretics should not corrupt and deprave them, as we gather had already happened from the book of the Constitutions attributed to the apostles, about which we shall speak more opportunely.

passages.original: Contra vero Chrysostomi ætate, quamvis Christiana religio huc illucque ibi- dem propagata fusset, eum magiæ et idololatriæ exitio (c), hec tamen ubique prorsus abolitat non erat, ob illarum gentium teritatem, quæ majorum in- stituta sequentes, soli summos honores tribuere non reformidabant, ut testatur ipsemet Chrysostomus hom. 11 ad populum Antiochenum. Neque tandem Beansorbe D. Hyde exagitare oportebat, quod Opus Imperfectum in Mathæum, veluti Chrystomi fetum landaverit. Illud enim plerique antiquorum Chryso- stomo adjudicarum ;
passages.english: On the contrary, in Chrysostom's age, although the Christian religion had been spread here and there in that same place, to the destruction of magic and idolatry, this [worship] had nevertheless not yet been entirely abolished everywhere, because of the savagery of those peoples, who, following the institutions of their ancestors, did not shrink from paying the highest honours to the sun, as Chrysostom himself testifies in Homily 11 to the people of Antioch. Nor, finally, was it right for Beausobre to attack Dr Hyde because he praised the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew as the offspring of Chrysostom. For most of the ancients assigned it to Chrysostom;
passages.notes: The text is badly scanned; read 'fuisset', 'in magiae et idololatriae exitium' (sense), 'haec', 'abolita', 'feritatem', 'soli' (the sun), 'Beausobre', 'Chrysostomi', 'laudaverit', 'adjudicarunt'. 'eum' is unclear and is taken as 'cum/in' with the sense 'to the destruction of'.

passages.original: Utrique autem Ecclesi æ nomen fuisse accommoda- tum quis ignora ? Quando igitur de Ecclesia in priori sensu accepta affirmatur hanc sine episcopo esse non potuisse, et unamque suum et unicum habuisse episcopum pr æsidentem, quem veteres, ut Justinus et Tertullianus summum sacerdotem appellarunt (c) id jam intelligi oportere de episcopatu secundum veterem et novam Ecclesiæ hierarchiam, omnibus exploratum esse debet. Quia vero Ecclesiæ, sic priori modo spectatæ, ut plurimum, tunc potissimum non angustis contrabebantur terminis, sed in longinqua spatia se extendebant, blures quandoque urbes, sub- urbia, pagos, castella, rura, idque genus alia com- prehendendo, non uniens pro omnibus hujus Eccle- siæ fidelibus sufficere poterat mysteriorum agendorum locus, nec unus sacerdos;
passages.english: Who does not know that the name "Church" was applied to both? When, therefore, it is affirmed of the Church taken in the former sense that it could not exist without a bishop, and that each had its own single bishop presiding, whom the ancients, such as Justin and Tertullian, called the high priest, it ought to be clear to all that this must be understood of the episcopate according to both the old and the new hierarchy of the Church. But because Churches regarded in the former way were, for the most part, especially at that time, not confined within narrow bounds but extended over distant spaces, sometimes comprising several cities, suburbs, villages, forts, country districts and other things of that kind, a single place for celebrating the mysteries could not suffice for all the faithful of such a Church, nor a single priest;
passages.notes: "uniens" read as "unicus"; "blures" as "plures".

passages.original: Secundo jam currente Ecclesiæ sæculo, et adhuc sævientibus, cum Judæorum, tum ethnicorum perse- cuionibus, ita Christianorum populous invreverat, ut non tantum in isignioribus urbibus, ut ait Eusebius, sed in oppidis et ruribus, Dominico die, omnes fide- les communiter conventum agerent, in quo Ecclesia- rum præpositi, sen præsidentes, rem divinam agebant. Quare si unicuique Ecclesiæ unicus tantum episcopus præerat (a), quemadmodum ex canonica Joannis Epistula compertum babemus, et ex episcoporum successionibus, ab Egesippo, Tertulliano, descriptis, intelligimus impossibile prorsus illi fuisse, eadem die, e loco in Iocum excurrere, totam diœcesim la- strare, et exspectata populi frequentia et multitudine eos conventus facere et absolvere, de quibus in præ- sentiarum sermo est.
passages.english: When the second century of the Church was already running, and the persecutions both of Jews and of pagans were still raging, the Christian people had so grown that not only in the more notable cities, as Eusebius says, but in towns and in the countryside, on the Lord's day all the faithful held an assembly in common, in which the heads or presidents of the Churches performed the divine service. Therefore, if only a single bishop presided over each Church, as we have learned from the canonical Epistle of John, and as we understand from the successions of bishops described by Hegesippus and Tertullian, it was altogether impossible for him on the same day to run from place to place, to go round the whole diocese, and, having waited for the people to gather in numbers, to hold and complete those assemblies of which we are now speaking.

passages.original: Et quia Deus et Dominum suscitavit, et nos cum illo suscitabit per virtutem suam (e). Decebat ergo ut Beausobre ubjecta nobis verba conferret cum reliquo disputationis (f) con- textu, et cum iis quæ ad Diodorum, seu Tryphonem presbyterum scripsit. Ibi enim, instituta compara- tione vetus inter testamantum et novum , utrumque a Deo esse ob summam prophetiarum consonantiam, multis exemplis in medium adductis, probat. Et lo- quens potissimum de Moyse, et Jesu, huc expresse sine ullo verborum involucro verum Moysis Domi- num appellat ; sabbati auctorem, beatitudinisque largi- torem Jesum esse affirm !at. Qui virtute propria educens populum e peccatorum vinculis, et captivitate, hunc æternæ tradidit saluti. Omnes quidem aliæque non absimiles loquendi formulæ, quemadmodum Jesum verum Dei Filium fuisse perspiene indicam, ita S.
passages.english: "And because God both raised up the Lord, and will raise us up with him by his power." Beausobre, then, ought to have compared the words set before us with the rest of the context of the disputation, and with what [Archelaus] wrote to Diodorus, or Trypho, the presbyter. For there, having drawn a comparison between the Old and the New Testament, he proves, bringing forward many examples, that both are from God because of the supreme agreement of the prophecies. And speaking especially of Moses and Jesus, he here expressly and without any veil of words calls [Jesus] the true Lord of Moses; he affirms that Jesus is the author of the sabbath and the giver of blessedness, "who, leading the people out by his own power from the chains and captivity of sins, delivered them to eternal salvation." All these and other not dissimilar formulas of speech, just as they clearly indicate that Jesus was the true Son of God, so [they show that] the holy
passages.notes: Breaks off mid-sentence ("S. episcopi" continues in context). "huc" perhaps for "hic"; "perspiene indicam" read as "perspicue indicant".

passages.original: Cujus quippe generis testi- monia, cum alia pene innumera in Scripturis fre- quentissime offendamus, quæ Filium Dei ex Maria natum binomine exprimunt, nuliam prorsus persona- rum distinctionem Jesum inter et Christum indican- tia haud video cur, qua religione, et quo nisu censor nus, de Præscriptionibus, cap. 47 ; Origenes, lib. VI contra Celsum : Iidem ! serpentem, a quo decepta fuit Eva, venerabantur, et Christum indigitalant noster existimare potuerit cam duabus illis vocibus simul copulatis Archelaum estruere, aut saltem in- nuere voluisse.
passages.english: Since we very frequently meet in the Scriptures almost countless other testimonies of this kind which express the Son of God born of Mary by a double name, indicating no distinction at all of persons between Jesus and Christ, I do not see why, by what scruple and by what effort, our critic could have thought that Archelaus, by joining those two words together, meant to build up, or at least hint at, [such a distinction].
passages.notes: The text is interrupted by an intruding footnote ("...[Tertullia]nus, On the Prescriptions, ch. 47; Origen, Against Celsus book 6: The same venerated the serpent by which Eve was deceived, and called it Christ"), omitted from the translation. "estruere" read as "astruere".

passages.original: Ex quibus omnibus illud consequitur, maxima injuria, in hæreseos suspicionem Archelaum fuisse adductum, quod utrumque momen Jesu et Christi Mariæ unico filio tribuerit. Hanc enum loquendi œco- nomiam cum servate oportuit, ut duarum naturarum conjunctionem indicaret, ut notat Theodoretus. Immo, auctore Augustino, si quis Jesum Christum plus quam hominem non novisset, Jesum Christum utique non novisset. Si enim tantummodo homo est, et nihil amplius, non est ipse Jesus Christus. Sed ad quam- cumque callidam atque fallacem Archelai verbis factam interpretationem penitus cripiendam, quid nobis opus esse potest aliorum catholicorum Patrum loquendi modo et sententiis ? Plenius semetipsum Archelaum explicasse, evidentissime produnt tum præfatæ disputationis argumenta et verboruml series et significatio, tum Manctis blasphemiæ et objecta quæ Scripturarum testimoniis rejicere et evertere S.
passages.english: From all of which it follows that it was a very great injustice that Archelaus was brought under suspicion of heresy because he attributed both names, Jesus and Christ, to the only son of Mary. For it was necessary to keep this arrangement of speech in order to indicate the union of the two natures, as Theodoret notes. Indeed, on Augustine's authority, if anyone had not known Jesus Christ as more than a man, he would certainly not have known Jesus Christ. For if he is only a man and nothing more, he is not Jesus Christ. But to remove entirely any crafty and deceitful interpretation made of Archelaus' words, what need can we have of the manner of speaking and the opinions of other catholic Fathers? That Archelaus explained himself more fully is shown most evidently both by the arguments of the aforesaid disputation and the sequence and meaning of its words, and by the blasphemies and objections of Manes which the holy
passages.notes: Breaks off mid-sentence ("S. episcopus conabatur" continues in context). "cripiendam" read as "eripiendam".

passages.original: Perperam tandem Epiphanius (addit) Manichæos stratos dormire atque cubare consuevisse supra paleas, aut spinas ; memoriam surpatriarchæ agentes, qui excoriatus fuerat spinarum acumine, ejusque pellem stramine aut paleis repletam. Sed id confinxisse Epiphanium, idem Beausobre, Augustini testimonio ductus, affirmat. Qui narrat schisina Romæ Manichæos inter exortum, quando Constantius Rom. civis, congregatis simul pluribus hujus sectæ homi- nibus, ut Manichaica adamussim præcepta observa- rent, quam citissime cœtus et congregatio illa in duas factiones divisa est.
passages.english: Finally, he adds, Epiphanius wrongly [says] that the Manichaeans were accustomed to sleep and lie stretched out on straw or thorns, keeping the memory of their patriarch, who had been flayed by the points of thorns, and whose skin [had been] stuffed with straw or chaff. But the same Beausobre, guided by the testimony of Augustine, asserts that Epiphanius invented this. [Augustine] relates that a schism arose among the Manichaeans at Rome when Constantius, a Roman citizen, gathered together a number of men of this sect so that they might observe the Manichaean precepts exactly; very quickly that assembly and congregation was split into two factions.
passages.notes: 'surpatriarchæ' read as 'sui patriarchae' (their patriarch). The sentence 'ejusque pellem stramine aut paleis repletam' is elliptical; a verb such as 'fuisse' is implied.

passages.original: sed cum scriptorem Mani- chæi discipulum ihi appellet, et de co tamquam de homine diu vita functo verba faciat, vix dubitare pos- sumus et Manetem audiisse, et, ejus parente, Adda nimirum, agente, inter secundi ordinis discipulos saltem locum obtinuisse (c). Sed et Adimanti Operum præterea idem Augustinus libro contra Faustum meminit. Primo quidem cum 119 sub istius nomine verba ponens, hunc Faustum, veluti de sua, Manetis et Adimanti doctrina gloriantem, quasi in scenam venire compellit, qui elatus insania audacius affirmabat : Satis superque jam in lucem traductis erroribus ac Judaicæ superstitionis simul, et semichristianorum abunde detecta fallacia, a dile- ctissimo, scilicet, et solo nobis post beatum Patrem nostrum Manichæum studioso Adimanto, non abs re visum est.
passages.english: But since he calls the writer a disciple of Mani there, and speaks of him as of a man long dead, we can hardly doubt that he both heard Mani and, through the agency of his parent, namely Adda, obtained a place at least among the disciples of the second rank (c). Moreover, the same Augustine also mentions the works of Adimantus in his book against Faustus. First, indeed, when, setting down words under that man's name, he makes this Faustus come as it were onto the stage, boasting of his own doctrine and that of Mani and Adimantus, who, carried away by madness, boldly declared: "Since the errors have now been more than sufficiently brought to light, and the deceit both of the Jewish superstition and of the half-Christians has been abundantly exposed by our most beloved Adimantus, the only [teacher] after our blessed Father Mani worthy of our study, it has not seemed inappropriate ..."
passages.notes: 'ihi' read as 'ibi', 'co' as 'eo'. The quotation breaks off at 'non abs re visum est' (continuing in the original Faustus). The phrase 'ejus parente, Adda nimirum' is odd ('his parent, Adda'); perhaps 'his patron/teacher' is meant; uncertain.

passages.original: Hoc autem contra Adimantum libro, totus est Augustinus in conciliandis inter se Scripturarum sen- tentiis, quas de Testamento vetere ac novo, velut in- vicem contrarias, idem Adimantus, utrumque Testa- mentum ab uno et eodem esse non posse conten- deus, eorraserat. Sed alterius libri a se ipso contra eumdem editi idem meminit Augustinus ; in quo pri- mum positis Admanti verbis, iisdem S. Pater suam reddiderat 120 responsionem. Quod opus, ait (e), uno volumine conclusi, et in eo quibusdam quæstionibus non semel, sed iterum respondi, quoniam quod primum respondi perierat, et tunc inventum est cum jam iterum respondissem, aliquas sane earumdem quæstionum po- pularibus ecclesiasticis sermonibus solvi, adhuc etiam aliquibus non respondu.
passages.english: In this book against Adimantus, Augustine is wholly occupied in reconciling with one another the statements of Scripture which the same Adimantus had scraped together from the Old and New Testaments as mutually contradictory, contending that the two Testaments cannot come from one and the same [author]. But the same Augustine mentions another book he himself published against the same man, in which, having first set down the words of Adimantus, the holy Father gave his reply to them. "This work," he says (e), "I enclosed in one volume, and in it I answered certain questions not once but twice, since what I first answered had been lost, and was found when I had already answered again; some of these same questions I resolved in popular church sermons, and to some I have still not replied."
passages.notes: 'eorraserat' read as 'corraserat'; 'respondu' as 'respondi'. The 'other book' framing is the author's; Augustine's quoted words seem to refer to the same work.

passages.original: martyris Justini querimoniam?Sibyllini enim libri apud eth- nicos erant in usu.In arduis enim aggrediendis re- bus vel expediendis Romani ipsi ad hos libros provo- cabant,ut inde subsidia haurirent.Quare ergo in im- perii negotiis præfa is libris fidem præsiabant .128 et in Christianæ religionis odium, quam obscure saltem vaticinabantur, in eos lantopere excanduerunt,ut ipsos disperderent? Arbitrabatur igitur Justinus hos libros ethnicis ipsis etiam subsidia exhibere posse ut lacilius Chisto nome, dorent. Siquidem tantam in eos liduciam habebant,auctore Tuo Livio (d): Ut ex senatus consulto,cum insnabili pernicici finis non in-reniretur, libri Sibyllini aditi sint. Justini ergo queri- monis non in en sit: erat, quod deperdita fuerint sacra monuments ad cathol cam fidem confirmandam apta et idonea;
passages.english: ...the complaint of the martyr Justin? For the Sibylline books were in use among the pagans. In undertaking or settling difficult matters the Romans themselves appealed to these books, to draw help from them. Why, then, did they trust these books in the affairs of the empire, and yet, out of hatred for the Christian religion, which they foretold at least obscurely, rage so fiercely against them as to destroy them? Justin therefore thought that these books could also offer the pagans themselves help toward giving their names to Christ more easily. For they had such confidence in them that, on the authority of Titus Livy (d), "by decree of the senate, when no end could be found to an incurable pestilence, the Sibylline books were consulted." Justin's complaint, then, was not that sacred records fit and suitable for confirming the catholic faith had been lost;
passages.notes: Heavy OCR damage: 'præsiabant' = praestabant, 'lacilius Chisto nome, dorent' = facilius Christo nomen darent, 'Tuo Livio' = Tito Livio, 'insnabili pernicici' = insanabili perniciei, 'aditi' = aditi; 'queri- monis non in en sit: erat' read as 'querimonia non in eo sita erat'.

passages.original: Nullum tamen cujusvis ordinis virum exstitisse, qui de talium librorum ja- ctura conquereretur, indicatum est. Persuasum illis quippe erat religionem novis et externis ritibus non esse attenuandam. Nam, auctore Cicerone, cultus deorum est optimus, idemque castissimus, atque san- ctissimus, plenissimusque pietatis, ut eos semper pura, integra et incorrupta mente et voce venere- mur (a). At quorsum mens atque vox peritatem, in- tegritatem institutorum ad rem sacram pertinentium servabunt, si vagari incipiant, et delectari in atiqui- bus soltem superstitiosis insolentissimisque rebus ?
passages.english: Yet it has been shown that there was no man of any order who complained of the loss of such books. For they were convinced that religion should not be weakened by new and foreign rites. For, on Cicero's authority, "the best worship of the gods, and likewise the most chaste, most holy and fullest of piety, is that we always revere them with a pure, whole and uncorrupted mind and voice" (a). But how will mind and voice preserve the purity and integrity of the institutions pertaining to sacred matters, if they begin to wander and to take delight in things at least somewhat superstitious and most unusual?
passages.notes: 'peritatem' read as 'puritatem'; 'atiqui- bus soltem' as 'aliquibus saltem'.

passages.original: Congressio isthæc igitur die se- quenti, id est septima Decembris, populo præsente, in ecclesia, cœpta est. Quam congressionem gesta eccle- siastica, seujudicium ecclesiasticum, a notariis quidem scripto consignatum, Augustinus appellat, quondam inter disputandum ab illa Manichæi epistola, quam fundamentum appellant, orsi sunt : sed non eadem die congressio hæc aut episcopalia Acta fuere abso- luta. Nam Felix cum veritate urgeretur, et Augustini argumentis maxime | erstringeretur, dixit : Dilationem peto, ut possim respondere.
passages.english: This meeting, then, began on the following day, that is the seventh of December, in the church, with the people present. Augustine calls this meeting the ecclesiastical proceedings, or ecclesiastical judgement, recorded in writing by notaries; once in the course of the debate they began from that letter of Mani which they call the Foundation. But this meeting, or the episcopal Acts, was not concluded on the same day. For Felix, pressed by the truth and hard bound by Augustine's arguments, said: "I ask for a postponement, so that I may be able to reply."
passages.notes: 'quondam' probably for 'quandoquidem' or 'quando'; read as 'since/when they began'. '| erstringeretur' = perstringeretur.

passages.original: Sed hoc maxime rogare, ut sibi Felici quo magis confirmaretur præiret Augustinus, ac Manichærum, necnon spiritum qui in eo locutus fuerat, prior annthemaret. Id tandem assecutus est. Nam accepta ab Augustino charta, anathematismo exsecravit; idem præstitit Felix verba sequential sua manu scribens : Ego Felix qui Manichæo crediderani, nunc anathemo eum et doctrinam ipsius; et id genus alia, quæ apud Augustinum in fine secundi libri com- mode ab omnibus pereurri possunt.
passages.english: But [he asked] above all this, that Augustine should go before him, Felix, so that he might be the more strengthened, and should first anathematise Mani and the spirit that had spoken in him. This he finally obtained. For taking the paper, Augustine cursed [them] with an anathema; Felix did the same, writing the following words with his own hand: "I, Felix, who had believed in Mani, now anathematise him and his doctrine," and other things of that kind, which anyone can conveniently read through in Augustine at the end of the second book.
passages.notes: 'Manichærum' = Manichaeum; 'crediderani' = credideram. The sequence (Augustine taking the paper) is somewhat unclear in the Latin.

passages.original: Tempo- rum enim injuria Acta ejusmodi a notariis excepta intercidere, et Augustinus aliunde et Prosper de qua- busdam mulieribus vitiatis dumtaxat facta mentione, reliquam gestorum seriem describere prætermise runt. In harum mulierum numerum duas potissimum retulit Augustinus. Alteram Margarita nominatam, quæ illam prodidit turpitudinem ; vedelicet, quæ cum esset annorum nondum duodecim propter hoc scelestum mysterium se dicebas esse vitiatam (a). Quod quidem flagitiosi propudii vitium cum pariter passa esset Eusebia quædam alia Manichæa femina, quasi sancti- monialis habita, eam vix compulit confiteri. Nam primo hæc se adhuc integrum retinere virginitatis florem perperam testabatur, atque ab obstetrice inspici po- stulabat.
passages.english: For through the injury of time such Acts, taken down by notaries, have perished, and Augustine elsewhere and Prosper, having merely mentioned certain women who were violated, omitted to describe the rest of the course of the proceedings. Among these women Augustine counted two in particular. One was named Margarita, who revealed that obscenity; namely, that when she was not yet twelve years old she said she had been violated for the sake of this wicked mystery (a). When a certain Eusebia, another Manichaean woman, regarded as a nun, had likewise suffered this vice of shameful outrage, she was barely compelled to confess it. For at first she falsely testified that she still kept the flower of her virginity intact, and asked to be examined by a midwife.
passages.notes: 'dicebas' read as 'dicebat'; 'integrum' with 'florem'.

passages.original: La- tinis doctior animoque perspicacior, Occidentalis Ecclesiæ oraculum, novem annorum spatio inter Ma- nichæos vitam egit, quin Manichæorum systema pe- netraverit? Poteratne Secundinus quid temerarius aut absurdius proferre? Alterutrum itaque (ait) di- cendum est: aut Augustinum non satis horum systema intellexisse; aut sanctum Augustinum illum mutasse, quod ab aliquibus sine hæreseos nota aftirmari haud posse arbitrabitur. Ego (subjicit) præ cæteris pluri- mum facio hujus Patris excellentes qualitates, non sine admiratione illius ingenium et sapientiam per- pendo, illius honoro memoriam, et diuturnos ejus labores existimo;
passages.english: [Did] the more learned of the Latins and keener in mind, the oracle of the Western Church, spend nine years among the Manichaeans without penetrating the Manichaean system? Could Secundinus have said anything more rash or absurd? "One of two things, therefore," he says, "must be said: either that Augustine did not sufficiently understand their system, or that Saint Augustine altered it"—which [Beausobre] will think cannot be asserted by some without the mark of heresy. "I," he adds, "value above all others the excellent qualities of this Father; I weigh his genius and wisdom not without admiration, I honour his memory, and I esteem his long labours;
passages.notes: 'temerarius' read as 'temerarius'/'temerarium'. The subject of 'arbitrabitur' is uncertain; taken as Beausobre.

passages.original: Fuit itaque tam solemnis, tam publica ipsorum Manichæorum confessio, et criminum detestatio, ut gestorum fama ad omnium Romanorum aures pervenire debuerit. Quamobrem cum hæc omnia in totius Ecclesiæ oculis Contigissent, ut scribit Prosper in sao Chronico, nemo sanæ mentis timere, aut dubitare poterat de illa sa- crorum præsulum potestate et jurisdictione, quam consules, quam senatores, quam denique imperator ipse communi consensione probaverant.
passages.english: So solemn, so public was the confession of the Manichaeans themselves and their repudiation of their crimes, that the report of the proceedings must have reached the ears of all Romans. Therefore, since all these things had happened before the eyes of the whole Church, as Prosper writes in his Chronicle, no one of sound mind could fear or doubt that power and jurisdiction of the holy prelates which the consuls, the senators, and finally the emperor himself had approved by common consent.

passages.original: Haudquaquam dubium esse potest quin mulieris nomine omnem femineum sexum ornesque ejus gradus Apostolus intellexerit. Quod quidem tum ipse totius Paulini canonis contextus imprimis probat, tum vero variis argumentis ex Scripturarum textibus depromptis Tertullianus demonstrat; gra vi censura præterea in eos invehens qui minus prudenter sibi persuasum voluere Paulum dumtaxat de nuptis mulieribus esse loculum, quique temerario quodam ausu contendebant innuptis mulieribus vel tonso capite, vel cincinnata corn , nullo prorsus assumpto clamine, tam sacris quam in civilihus conventibus prodire esse licitum, prætextu quandoque falsæ virginitatis magnifice jactandæ ac ostentandae.
passages.english: There can be no doubt at all that by the word "woman" the Apostle understood the whole female sex and all its ranks. This is proved above all by the context of the entire Pauline canon itself, and Tertullian also demonstrates it with various arguments drawn from the texts of Scripture; he moreover inveighs with severe censure against those who, with too little prudence, wished to persuade themselves that Paul had spoken only of married women, and who with a certain rash daring contended that it was lawful for unmarried women to appear, whether with shorn head or with curled hair, with no covering at all, in sacred as well as in civil assemblies, sometimes on the pretext of magnificently boasting and displaying a false virginity.
passages.notes: "ornesque" read as "omnesque"; "gra vi" as "gravi"; "loculum" as "locutum"; "corn" probably "coma" (hair); "clamine" as "velamine" (covering); "civilihus" as "civilibus".

passages.original: Non itaque apposite ratiocinatur Ludovicus Capelfus cum laudato loco ait apostoli Pauli tempore hoc unum fuisse receptum, et in more positum, ut ca- stæ et pudicæ mulieres, præsertim- nubiles, vix umquam in publicum nisi velata facie prodirent; tum ad Judæorum gentem sermonem convertens, subdit: Nescio att forte judaica excipi debeat. Hæc porro, Tertulliano auctore, excipi non poterat, cum Judæorum Ecclesia naquaquam civili consuetudine innixa (quemadmodum barbaræ nationes), sed 201 Spiritus sancti traditione edocta semper prosecuta sit quidquid foret patrocinaturum pudori et verecundiæ feminei sexus.
passages.english: Louis Cappel therefore does not reason fittingly when he says, in the passage cited, that in the time of the apostle Paul this alone was accepted and established as custom, that chaste and modest women, especially marriageable ones, scarcely ever went out in public except with veiled face; and then, turning his discussion to the Jewish nation, he adds: "I do not know whether perhaps the Jewish [nation] ought to be excepted." This, however, on Tertullian's authority, could not be excepted, since the Church of the Jews, relying by no means on civil custom (as the barbarian nations did), but taught by the tradition of the Holy Spirit, always pursued whatever would protect the modesty and shamefastness of the female sex.
passages.notes: "Capelfus" read as "Capellus" (Louis Cappel); "att" as "an"; "naquaquam" as "nequaquam". "201" is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: Ut videlicet mulieres discerent studio et arte ea tegenda esse, quæ natura tegere voluit, atque eo assumpto velamine in memoriam revocarent primam muliebris conditionis rationem, propter quam Evae omnibusque feminis, Gen. III, 16, dictum fuit : Et sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui. Quae saue verba non ad solam dilectionis subjectionem, sed ad earum conditionem referenda esse, inter cætcros PP. unus docuit (f) Augustinus lib. xi de Genesi ad Lit., quatenus vir etiam mulieri nolenti debeat dominari, ut nisi hoc dominium servetur depra- vabitur .amplius natura et augebitur culpa.
passages.english: [This was] so that women might learn that what nature wished to cover must be covered by effort and art, and that, having put on that veil, they might call to mind the first principle of the female condition, on account of which it was said to Eve and to all women (Gen. 3:16): "And you shall be under the power of the man, and he shall rule over you." That these words are indeed to be referred not only to the subjection of love but to their condition, Augustine among the other Fathers taught, in book 11 of On Genesis according to the Letter, inasmuch as the man must rule the woman even against her will, so that unless this dominion is preserved, nature will be further depraved and guilt increased.
passages.notes: "saue" read as "sane"; "cætcros PP." as "ceteros Patres"; "(f)" is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Quem ritum gentiles servasse, probat Aristophanes, qui admiratione quasi captus cuidam servo comam nutrienti olim dixit: Servus cum sis comam nutris? Capillorum item tonsio multorum sive graviorum criminum pœna fnit, scribente etiam Apostolo, v. G laudati cap. : Si non velatur mulier, tondeatur, quasi ut in pœnam violatæ legis de gestando velamine mulier ipsa tonderi debeat et decalvari. Sed et alia crimina eamdem dccalvationis pcenain subiisse, non tantum ex variis Seripturarum locis, sed ex civilibus legibus apud Ulpianum, Justinianum, Tacitum colligimus. Ad quem ritum Juvenalem alludere voluisse arbitror satira 5, qui scripsit (d) : ,...Pulsandum vertice raso Praebebit quandoque caput, nec dura timebit Flagra pati.
passages.english: That the gentiles kept this custom is proved by Aristophanes, who, as though seized with astonishment, once said to a certain slave who was growing his hair: "Though you are a slave, you grow your hair long?" Likewise the cutting of the hair was the punishment for many or graver crimes, as the Apostle also writes in verse 6 of the chapter cited: "If a woman is not veiled, let her be shorn," as if, as a penalty for violating the law on wearing the veil, the woman herself ought to be shorn and made bald. But that other crimes too incurred the same penalty of shaving, we gather not only from various passages of Scripture but from civil laws, in Ulpian, Justinian, and Tacitus. I think Juvenal meant to allude to this custom in Satire 5, where he wrote: "...With his crown shaved, he will at some time offer his head to be struck, and will not fear to suffer the harsh whips."
passages.notes: "v. G" read as "v. 6"; "fnit" as "fuit"; "(d)" a footnote mark.

passages.original: Quos inter Hieronymus, Ambrosius, Augustinus (e), quorum testimomis Baromus in Martyrologio insistit, ad dicrn 20 Septembris, sanctae Faustae virginis martyrium describens. Eam quoque turpitudinem profani scriptores exaggerant, ut videre est apud Apuleium, Sta- tium, Virgilium, aliosque, quibus subscribens Ovidius ita cecinit : Turpe pecus mutilum, turpis sine gramine campus Et sine fronde frutex, et siue crino caput. Has praecedentes rationes qnarta excipit, quæ ex pœnitentia luctu, atque 204 mœrore desumpta est. Notissimum quippe omnibus esse debet, consuevisse Judaeos atque gentiles in luctu maximisque funeribus sihi comas tondere.
passages.english: Among them [are] Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine, on whose testimonies Baronius relies in the Martyrology at 20 September, describing the martyrdom of the holy virgin Fausta. Profane writers also exaggerate this disgrace, as can be seen in Apuleius, Statius, Virgil and others; agreeing with them, Ovid sang thus: "Ugly is a maimed beast, ugly a field without grass, and a shrub without leaves, and a head without hair." A fourth reason follows these preceding ones, which is taken from penitence, grief and mourning. For it must be very well known to all that Jews and gentiles were accustomed to cut their hair in mourning and at the greatest funerals.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (testimoniis, Baronius, diem, sine crine, quarta, sibi); "204" is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: nunc autem ne meo abuti otio vestraque eruditione diffidere videar, reliqua persequar, quae duo postrema meæ dissertationis capita expedire possunt. De miraque eniin tum sacrarum litterarum inLerpretes, tum summi theologi jam pridem disserucrunt, ut videre cst apud Ambrosium, Hieronymum, Augustinum, vel apud Gulielmum Parisiensem, Doctorem Angelicum , Nicolaum de Ausmo , caeterosque etiamtheologiæ moralis scriptores; quorum catalogus in nostrum scopum nihil conferret.
passages.english: but now, lest I seem to abuse my leisure and to distrust your learning, I shall pursue the remaining matters, which the last two heads of my dissertation can settle. For on both, interpreters of Sacred Scripture as well as the greatest theologians have long since discoursed, as can be seen in Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, or in William of Paris, the Angelic Doctor, Nicholas of Osimo, and the other writers on moral theology too; a catalogue of whom would contribute nothing to our purpose.
passages.notes: "De miraque" read as "De utraque" (on both); "Ausmo" taken as Auximo (Osimo).

passages.original: ex numismatibus pariter, annulorumque signis probare possemus promistuam illam vestimentorum confusionem longe post Moysis aetatem in orbem invectam fuisse. Forte eam primi omnium Cyprii excogitarunt, cum in templo Άϕροδίτου statua collocata, quae Venerem significabat, cui viri in mulietri, et mutieres in virili veste sacrificabant, ut Servius tradit. Dere Isidis sacerdotibus pariter Romae solemne fuit muliebribus indui vestimentis, ut prodit anaglyphum Capitolinum, eruditissime a clarissimo. viroGeorgio illustratum. Introductis item ex Græcia in Etruriam, et Italiam potissimum, Bacchanalibus festis, frequentior fuit in viris et mulieribus promiscua illa vestium usurpatio, et Romae primum contigit, annu conditæ Urbis quingentesimo sexto, ante Christum natum centesimo octuagesimo nono, ut auctor est Titus Livius, et Romanorum consulum tabulæ patefaciunt (e).
passages.english: [...] from coins likewise, and from the devices of signet rings, we could prove that that promiscuous confusion of garments was introduced into the world long after the age of Moses. Perhaps the Cypriots first of all devised it, when a statue of Aphroditus was set up in a temple, which signified Venus, to whom men sacrificed in women's dress and women in men's dress, as Servius relates. Likewise, at Rome it was customary for the priests of Isis to put on women's garments, as a Capitoline relief shows, most learnedly illustrated by the most distinguished man Giorgi. Likewise, when the Bacchanalian festivals had been introduced from Greece into Etruria and above all into Italy, that promiscuous use of garments by men and women became more frequent, and it first occurred at Rome in the five hundred and sixth year from the founding of the City, one hundred and eighty-ninth before the birth of Christ, as Titus Livy reports and the tables of the Roman consuls reveal.
passages.notes: The sentence begins mid-clause, continuing from the context ('from mosaics, statues, reliefs...'). Scanning errors corrected: 'promiscuam', 'muliebri', 'mulieres', 'De', 'anno'. 'Georgio' taken as the scholar Giorgi; identification uncertain. The figures 506 A.U.C. and 189 B.C. do not correspond (568 A.U.C. = 186 B.C.); translated as printed.

passages.original: Fit enim in ea veslimentoruu: promiscua confusione quædam meulila sexuum perinutatio a Cræcis γενέσεως ὲναλλαγή dicta (ut Grutius animadvertit) quæ omnibus naturae ofnciis repugnat. Propterea, quemadmodum virorum auctoritas et majestas læditur si muliebria opera facere velint, ut olim Clemens Alexandrinus annotavit (e), ita injusto arrogantine et audaciæ jure se mulier extollit, quando motu, indumentis, incessu atque operibus allis, viros imitari et simulare studet. Huic .porro agendi vivendique rationi, venias, justitia et honestas repugnant.
passages.english: For in it, through the indiscriminate confusion of garments, there takes place a certain lying exchange of the sexes, called by the Greeks genéseōs enallagḗ ["exchange of kind"] (as Grotius observes), which is contrary to all the duties of nature. Therefore, just as the authority and dignity of men is injured if they wish to do women's work, as Clement of Alexandria once noted, so a woman exalts herself by an unjust right of arrogance and audacity when she strives to imitate and feign men in movement, clothing, gait and other actions. To this manner of acting and living, moreover, [nature's] laws, justice and decency are opposed.
passages.notes: "meulila ... perinutatio" read as "mendax ... permutatio"; "Grutius" as Grotius; "venias" unclear, perhaps "naturae iura" (cf. following context), tentatively rendered.

passages.original: Et quidem ejusmodi mala, aut alia quædam etiam graviora, ex illa promiscusa vestium permutatione evenire possunt; ideo, spectata saniori disserendi ratione, censemus Denteronomii preceptum non primario ad exterminandos idololatricos ritus, sed ad humanos mores moderandus datum fuisse. Et quidem, Ambrosio auctore, hominum mores semper turpes et abominabiles lUunt, ubi dirigantur a studio celandi et occultandi sexum (g) : Mendacium et turpe in verbis est, nedumin habitu. Cyprianus quoque tum viros quam mulieres qui hisce abusibus vacant viluti adultcrus reprehendit: Manus Deo inferunt, quoniam itlud quod ille formavit reformare contendunt.
passages.english: And indeed such evils, or certain others even graver, can arise from that indiscriminate exchange of garments; therefore, considering the sounder way of reasoning, we judge that the precept of Deuteronomy was given not primarily to exterminate idolatrous rites, but to regulate human morals. And indeed, on Ambrose's authority, human conduct is always shameful and abominable when it is directed by the desire to conceal and hide one's sex: "A lie is shameful in words, still more in dress." Cyprian also reproves both men and women who give themselves to these abuses as adulterers: "They lay hands on God, since they strive to re-form what he formed."
passages.notes: "lUunt" read as "fiunt"; "adultcrus" as "adulteros"; "(g)" a footnote mark.
